prompt: A company runs an on-premises data center and wants a dedicated, private connection to Google Cloud with tens of Gbps of bandwidth that does **not** traverse the public internet. They want the topology for which Google publishes a 99.99% availability SLA. Which approach should the architect recommend?

choices.text: A single Dedicated Interconnect connection terminated at one edge location, with one VLAN attachment and a single Cloud Router
choices.rationale: A single connection is a single point of failure at the facility and edge availability domain level, so it cannot qualify for the 99.99% topology.

choices.text: Dedicated Interconnect with four connections, two in each of two metros and spread across both edge availability domains, plus two Cloud Routers
choices.rationale: Google's 99.99% Dedicated Interconnect topology needs at least four connections (two in each of two metros, in different edge availability domains), at least four VLAN attachments across two regions, and a Cloud Router in each region.

choices.text: HA VPN with one tunnel on each gateway interface, using BGP sessions on a Cloud Router across the public internet
choices.rationale: HA VPN can carry a 99.99% SLA, but its encrypted tunnels still cross the public internet, which the stated requirement rules out.

choices.text: Partner Interconnect with a single VLAN attachment provisioned through one service provider in a single metro area
choices.rationale: Partner Interconnect is private, but a single VLAN attachment has no redundancy; its 99.99% topology needs four attachments across two metros with two Cloud Routers.

explanation: Redundancy for the SLA is counted in connections, metros, edge availability domains and Cloud Routers, not in circuit size.

prompt: An architect is designing connectivity so that workloads in a consumer VPC can reach a SaaS provider's service and a published Google API **privately**, without external IPs and without VPC Peering's transitivity limits. Which statements about Private Service Connect (PSC) are correct? Choose two.

choices.text: PSC endpoints or backends can target supported Google APIs, so API traffic uses internal IP addresses instead of public ones
choices.rationale: Endpoints and backends can target Google APIs, giving granular IP control as an alternative to Private Google Access.

choices.text: PSC makes routes transitive across every VPC peered with the consumer network, so shared services are reachable organization-wide
choices.rationale: PSC exchanges no routes and is not a transitivity mechanism; access is granted per service through explicit accept lists.

choices.text: PSC endpoints must be assigned external IP addresses so the producer's load balancer can accept the consumer's connections
choices.rationale: Endpoints use internal IP addresses from the consumer VPC; the point of PSC is to avoid public addressing.

choices.text: A consumer creates an internal endpoint (a forwarding rule with an internal IP address) that maps to the producer's published service
choices.rationale: PSC endpoints are deployed as forwarding rules that give the consumer an internal IP address mapped to the producer's service attachment.

choices.text: PSC requires the consumer and producer VPC networks to be connected by VPC Network Peering before an endpoint can reach the service
choices.rationale: PSC is service-oriented: traffic targets a single service IP and each side is isolated by NAT, so no peering of the two networks is needed.

explanation: Prefer PSC over peering when you want one-directional, per-service access with no route leakage between networks.

prompt: A global web application serves HTTPS traffic to users worldwide. The architect needs a single anycast IP, TLS termination at the edge, URL-based routing to different backend services, and integration with Cloud CDN. Which load balancer is the correct choice?

choices.text: Regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer, with one regional IP address for the backends in a single region
choices.rationale: It is Layer 4 and regional: no TLS termination, no URL maps, no Cloud CDN, and no single global anycast address.

choices.text: Global external Application Load Balancer, with one anycast IP address, edge TLS termination and URL maps
choices.rationale: It is the Layer 7 global option: one anycast IP, TLS termination at distributed edge locations, URL-based routing, Cloud CDN support and multi-region backends.

choices.text: Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer, with a private regional IP address reachable only from inside the VPC network
choices.rationale: It is internal and regional, so it cannot serve internet users and offers no TLS termination, URL routing or CDN.

choices.text: Regional internal Application Load Balancer, with a private IP address, TLS termination and URL maps in one region
choices.rationale: It has Layer 7 features but is internal and regional, with no Cloud CDN support and no global anycast address for worldwide users.

explanation: Pair the global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Armor and Cloud CDN for edge protection and caching.

prompt: A security team wants to apply consistent, hierarchical firewall rules across an entire folder of projects, and separately wants managed intrusion detection (threat detection for malware, spyware and command-and-control traffic) on its VPC traffic. Which combination correctly maps the requirements to Google Cloud features?

choices.text: Hierarchical firewall policies for intrusion detection; Cloud NAT gateways to provide the folder-wide rule hierarchy
choices.rationale: Firewall policies allow, deny or pass traffic; they do not inspect payloads for threats. Cloud NAT translates egress addresses and has no policy hierarchy.

choices.text: Cloud Armor policies for the folder-wide hierarchy; VPC Service Controls perimeters for packet-level intrusion detection
choices.rationale: Cloud Armor policies attach to backend services, not folders. VPC Service Controls limit API-level data exfiltration and do not inspect packets.

choices.text: VPC firewall rules configured separately in each project for the hierarchy; Cloud Armor security policies for intrusion detection
choices.rationale: VPC firewall rules apply to a single network and are not inherited from a folder; Cloud Armor protects internet-facing load balancers and is not an intrusion detection service.

choices.text: Hierarchical firewall policies associated with the folder; Cloud IDS for managed intrusion detection on mirrored traffic
choices.rationale: Hierarchical policies associate with an organization or folder and cascade to child projects. Cloud IDS analyzes mirrored traffic with Palo Alto Networks threat detection and alerts on intrusions.

explanation: Cloud IDS only detects and alerts; pair it with Cloud NGFW rules if traffic must be blocked.

prompt: Logs are written to a Cloud Storage bucket and read heavily for 30 days, occasionally for the next 11 months, and almost never afterward, but they must be retained for 7 years for compliance. The architect wants to minimize cost while keeping the data in one bucket. What is the best configuration?

choices.text: Keep every object in Standard storage for its entire life and delete objects once they reach 7 years of age
choices.rationale: Standard has the highest storage price, and nearly all of the 7 years is spent on data that is almost never read.

choices.text: Use Object Lifecycle Management to move objects to Nearline at 30 days and Archive at one year, deleting them after 7 years
choices.rationale: Age-based SetStorageClass rules match the access curve: Standard while hot, Nearline (30-day minimum) for occasional reads, Archive (365-day minimum) for the long tail, then a Delete rule.

choices.text: Write every object directly to Archive storage on day one, because it has the lowest per-GiB storage price of any class
choices.rationale: Archive has retrieval fees and a 365-day minimum duration, so the heavily read first month would be expensive and early deletion would be charged.

choices.text: Enable Autoclass with Nearline as the terminal class, so that objects are never moved into colder and cheaper classes
choices.rationale: With the default Nearline terminal class, objects never reach Archive pricing, so the long tail stays more expensive than a deliberate Archive transition.

explanation: Add a locked retention policy as well if objects must be undeletable for the 7 years; lifecycle Delete is skipped while a retention policy is unmet.

prompt: An auditor requires that financial records in Cloud Storage be immutable and undeletable for exactly 5 years (WORM compliance), and that nobody, including project owners, can shorten the retention window. Which controls achieve this? Choose two.

choices.text: Set a bucket retention policy of 5 years, so objects cannot be deleted or replaced until each one is 5 years old
choices.rationale: A retention policy sets the minimum age before deletion or replacement and applies retroactively to existing objects, failing attempts with retentionPolicyNotMet.

choices.text: Enable Object Versioning and rely on soft delete so that any deleted or overwritten data can always be recovered later
choices.rationale: Versioning and soft delete recover mistakes but do not enforce a regulatory window; versions can still be removed and soft-deleted data expires after its own retention duration.

choices.text: Lock the retention policy (Bucket Lock), which stops it from being reduced or removed even by project owners
choices.rationale: Once locked, a policy cannot be removed or shortened (it can only be increased), which is what turns the retention window into WORM protection.

choices.text: Grant only the project owner the storage.admin role and instruct them in writing never to delete the financial records
choices.rationale: A written instruction is not a technical control, and an owner can still delete objects or change permissions.

choices.text: Apply an IAM deny policy that blocks every read of the bucket for 5 years so that the stored data stays untouched
choices.rationale: Denying reads blocks the auditors, does not prevent deletion or overwrite, and can itself be altered by administrators.

prompt: An architect must transfer 300 TB of archival video from an on-premises NAS to Cloud Storage within five weeks. The site has a 1 Gbps internet link, roughly 70% of which production traffic already uses. What is the most appropriate transfer method?

choices.text: Run gcloud storage uploads with parallel composite uploads over the existing 1 Gbps link, throttled to protect production traffic
choices.rationale: At 1 Gbps even a fully idle link moves roughly 10 TB a day; with only about 30% free, 300 TB would take months, so tuning the uploader cannot meet the deadline.

choices.text: Use Storage Transfer Service with agents on the NAS to copy the data over the public internet during off-peak hours
choices.rationale: Storage Transfer Service speeds up and manages online copies, but the data still crosses the same constrained link.

choices.text: Order Transfer Appliance, copy the data locally at LAN speed, and ship the appliance to Google for upload to Cloud Storage
choices.rationale: Google's guidance suits Transfer Appliance when a network upload would take over a week; capturing 300 TB takes under 25 days including shipping, independent of the shared link.

choices.text: Provision a Dedicated Interconnect circuit first and then copy the data with gcloud storage over the new private connection
choices.rationale: A circuit takes lead time to order and cross-connect, and it adds standing cost for a one-time copy when an offline path already fits the deadline.

explanation: Compare the transfer time on the usable bandwidth against the deadline: when it exceeds about a week, an offline appliance is the usual answer.

prompt: A batch image-rendering pipeline is fault-tolerant, checkpoints frequently, and can restart interrupted tasks. The team wants the lowest possible compute cost on Compute Engine and accepts that instances may be reclaimed at any time. Which provisioning model should they use?

choices.text: Sole-tenant nodes that reserve dedicated physical servers for the rendering workload and its licensing needs
choices.rationale: Sole-tenant nodes serve isolation and licensing needs at higher cost, and Spot VMs cannot run on them at all.

choices.text: Reserved capacity bought with a three-year commitment sized for the peak rendering fleet, paid whether used or not
choices.rationale: A long commitment suits predictable always-on load, the opposite of interruptible batch work that wants the cheapest price.

choices.text: Standard on-demand VMs covered by committed use discounts that are sized to the average rendering load
choices.rationale: Commitments cut the price of steady usage but cost far more than Spot, and the team is paying for capacity an interruptible job does not need.

choices.text: Spot VMs in a managed instance group that recreates preempted instances when capacity returns
choices.rationale: Spot VMs give discounts of up to 91% with no SLA, which suits checkpointed, restartable work, and a MIG keeps the group at its target size by recreating preempted VMs.

explanation: Enable the 120-second preemption notice (default is none) so tasks can checkpoint before shutdown.

prompt: A team wants Kubernetes on Google Cloud but does not want to manage node pools, node upgrades, capacity planning, or bin-packing; they want to pay per-Pod resource request and have Google operate the nodes. Which option fits best?

choices.text: GKE Standard with node auto-provisioning, which creates node pools automatically as Pod demand changes
choices.rationale: Standard still leaves node configuration and upgrades with the team and bills for whole nodes rather than for Pod requests.

choices.text: GKE Autopilot, where Google manages the nodes and billing follows the resources that the Pods request
choices.rationale: In Autopilot, GKE manages nodes and scaling and provisions compute to match workload specifications, so you pay for Pod resource requests.

choices.text: Self-managed Kubernetes with kubeadm on Compute Engine VMs, with the team operating the control plane itself
choices.rationale: Self-managing maximizes the operational burden, including control plane upgrades, node capacity and bin-packing.

choices.text: Knative serving installed on a cluster that the team operates, so the platform handles Pod autoscaling
choices.rationale: A serverless layer on a user-managed cluster still leaves the cluster, node pools and upgrades with the team.

explanation: Choose Standard instead when you need privileged workloads or granular control over node configuration.

prompt: A stateless containerized REST API has spiky traffic, must scale to zero when idle, and should scale out automatically based on concurrent requests with minimal infrastructure management. The team already builds OCI container images. What is the best fit?

choices.text: GKE Standard with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, running node pools that the team sizes and upgrades
choices.rationale: Standard clusters require node pool management and keep nodes running, which conflicts with scale to zero and minimal infrastructure management.

choices.text: The App Engine flexible environment, with containers running on always-on VMs that the platform manages
choices.rationale: Flexible runs containers on Compute Engine VMs and keeps a minimum of one instance running, so it cannot scale to zero.

choices.text: Cloud Run services, with request-driven autoscaling and the minimum instance count left at its default of zero
choices.rationale: Cloud Run scales out on incoming requests and concurrency, and a minimum of zero (the default) lets it scale in to nothing when idle.

choices.text: A Compute Engine managed instance group with autoscaling, using VM images that the team builds, patches and maintains
choices.rationale: A MIG leaves the team with VM image lifecycle and slower VM start-up, so spiky container traffic is neither as hands-off nor as fast to scale as Cloud Run.

explanation: Use Cloud Run jobs for run-to-completion batch work, and tune concurrency to trade cost against latency.

prompt: An enterprise wants to lift-and-shift its VMware vSphere estate to Google Cloud with minimal changes, keeping vCenter, vSAN, and NSX, while gaining a path to modernize later. Which service is designed for this?

choices.text: Migrate to Virtual Machines, converting each VMware VM into a native Compute Engine instance after replication
choices.rationale: Migration converts VMs into Compute Engine instances, which is re-platforming away from vCenter, vSAN and NSX rather than keeping them.

choices.text: Google Cloud VMware Engine, a managed VMware environment running on dedicated bare metal nodes in Google Cloud
choices.rationale: VMware Engine runs vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX and HCX on dedicated, physically isolated bare metal, so the estate moves with minimal change.

choices.text: GKE on VMware clusters (formerly Anthos clusters on VMware), running Kubernetes on the existing on-premises vSphere hosts
choices.rationale: That product runs Kubernetes on VMware in your own data center; it does not relocate a vSphere estate into Google Cloud.

choices.text: Bare Metal Solution, providing dedicated servers in a regional extension for specialized workloads such as Oracle databases
choices.rationale: Bare Metal Solution supplies specialized bare metal servers, not a managed VMware environment with vCenter, vSAN and NSX.

explanation: Naming of the Anthos-era and Bare Metal Solution distractors was not re-verified against current docs; their roles as distractors do not depend on it.

prompt: An architect is standardizing infrastructure as code on Google Cloud and wants a managed way to run Terraform, with previews before changes apply, while also offering teams reusable, validated blueprints. Which statements are accurate? Choose two.

choices.text: Deployment Manager is the recommended infrastructure-as-code service for new projects and still gets ongoing feature investment
choices.rationale: Deployment Manager reached end of support on March 31, 2026; Google points users to Infrastructure Manager or other Terraform tooling.

choices.text: Terraform state should always be kept on each engineer's laptop so that no remote system holds sensitive resource data
choices.rationale: Local state breaks collaboration and locking and risks loss; shared state belongs in a remote, access-controlled backend.

choices.text: Config Connector cannot manage Google Cloud resources from Kubernetes and works only with other cloud providers' APIs
choices.rationale: Config Connector is a Kubernetes add-on that manages Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources.

choices.text: Infrastructure Manager is a managed service that deploys Terraform configurations and can create preview deployments before applying
choices.rationale: It runs Terraform as deployments and revisions, sourced from Cloud Storage, Git or local directories, and supports previews.

choices.text: Terraform blueprints package reusable modules and policy into opinionated, deployable solutions that follow Google-recommended designs
choices.rationale: Blueprints are described as packages of deployable, reusable modules and policy implementing a specific opinionated solution.

explanation: The old stem listed drift detection and policy enforcement as Infrastructure Manager features; the current overview does not document them, so they are no longer asserted.

prompt: A fleet of hundreds of Compute Engine VMs in a single project needs scheduled OS patching with reporting on which VMs are compliant, plus the ability to run pre- and post-patch scripts. Which Google Cloud capability should the architect use?

choices.text: Connect to each VM over SSH and run the distribution package manager by hand on a rotating weekly schedule
choices.rationale: Manual SSH does not scale to hundreds of VMs and produces no compliance reporting.

choices.text: VM Manager patch management, with scheduled deployments, maintenance windows and a compliance dashboard
choices.rationale: VM Manager patch uses the OS Config agent for one-time or recurring deployments with maintenance windows and pre/post scripts, and its dashboard reports compliance.

choices.text: Cloud Build triggers that bake a fresh custom image and recreate the whole VM fleet from it every night
choices.rationale: Rebuilding every VM nightly is disruptive and wasteful; image baking suits golden images, not routine patching of a running fleet.

choices.text: Cloud Scheduler jobs that call the Compute Engine API to reset every VM on a fixed schedule each night
choices.rationale: A reset restarts the machine but installs no patches and reports nothing about compliance.

explanation: Patch jobs run only for VMs in a single project, so a multi-project fleet needs a separate deployment per project.

prompt: A data science team wants to orchestrate a repeatable ML workflow — data preprocessing, training, evaluation, and conditional model deployment — as a managed, serverless, reproducible DAG on Google Cloud's AI platform (the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI). Which component should they use?

choices.text: Cloud Run functions chained manually through Pub/Sub topics, with one function for each stage of the workflow
choices.rationale: Chained functions are brittle to operate and give no ML artifact or metadata lineage or step caching.

choices.text: BigQuery scheduled queries that run SQL statements on a recurring schedule to stand in for each workflow stage
choices.rationale: Scheduled queries run SQL on a timer; they do not orchestrate training, evaluation and deployment steps as a DAG.

choices.text: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines (formerly Vertex AI Pipelines), built with the Kubeflow Pipelines SDK or TFX
choices.rationale: Pipelines orchestrates ML workflows serverlessly as a DAG, with artifact lineage tracking and execution caching so unchanged steps are skipped.

choices.text: A single long-running Compute Engine VM that runs a bash script for each stage of the workflow in order, keeping state on local disk
choices.rationale: A hand-rolled script on one VM has no managed orchestration, caching or lineage, and the VM is a single point of failure.

explanation: The platform was previously named Vertex AI; the current docs title the feature Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines.

prompt: A research team is training a very large foundation model that needs thousands of accelerators with high-bandwidth interconnect and a tightly co-located, dense compute fabric optimized for large-scale training and inference. Which Google Cloud offering describes this integrated supercomputing architecture, and what accelerator is purpose-built by Google for it?

choices.text: AI Hypercomputer, which integrates TPUs and GPUs with high-bandwidth networking, storage and optimized open software
choices.rationale: AI Hypercomputer is Google's integrated supercomputing system for AI: TPUs and NVIDIA GPUs, networking and storage, open frameworks, and flexible consumption such as reservations and Dynamic Workload Scheduler.

choices.text: A fleet of general-purpose CPU VMs on the default network, training with generic data-parallel software and no accelerators
choices.rationale: CPU-only VMs on a standard network lack the accelerators and interconnect needed for foundation-model training at scale.

choices.text: Cloud Run jobs with CPU-only autoscaling, splitting the training dataset across many short-lived containers
choices.rationale: Short-lived CPU containers have neither accelerators nor the tightly coupled, high-bandwidth fabric that distributed training needs.

choices.text: Persistent Disk snapshots restored onto many VMs in parallel to speed up the training of the large model
choices.rationale: Snapshots are backups; restoring them adds no compute acceleration and does not provide an accelerator fabric.

explanation: Google's purpose-built accelerator in this architecture is the Cloud TPU; NVIDIA GPUs are supported alongside it.

prompt: A product team wants to add AI features quickly without training models from scratch. Which statements about Google Cloud's prebuilt AI and model options are accurate? Choose two.

choices.text: Model Garden is a hub where teams discover, test, deploy and tune Google, open and partner models
choices.rationale: Model Garden is the central hub within the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform for first-party (Gemini), open and partner models.

choices.text: The Cloud Vision API offers label detection, OCR, object localization and SafeSearch as pretrained features with no custom training
choices.rationale: These Vision API features are ready to use through an API call; custom training is only needed for specialized detection.

choices.text: Prebuilt APIs such as Vision and Speech-to-Text require the customer to provision and operate their own GPU clusters
choices.rationale: Prebuilt APIs are fully managed endpoints; the customer provisions no accelerators.

choices.text: NotebookLM is a low-level block storage product that attaches disks to Compute Engine VMs for AI datasets
choices.rationale: NotebookLM is an AI research and note-taking assistant, not an infrastructure storage product.

choices.text: Calling a prebuilt API is free of charge regardless of request volume, because Google hosts the models itself
choices.rationale: Prebuilt APIs are consumed as metered managed services, so cost grows with usage rather than staying at zero.

explanation: Start with prebuilt APIs for common tasks; move to Model Garden models or tuning when the task needs customization.

prompt: Altostrat Media streams video globally and is consolidating multiple business units, each with its own project and VPC and overlapping RFC 1918 ranges, into one network. They accept re-addressing workloads into a single planned address space. They want the network team to control subnets and firewall policy centrally, while application teams deploy in their own projects on that shared network. Which design should the architect recommend?

choices.text: A Shared VPC, where a host project owns the VPC, subnets and firewalls while service projects attach and deploy into them
choices.rationale: Shared VPC separates central network ownership (host project) from workload ownership (service projects) on one network with one address plan.

choices.text: VPC Network Peering between every pair of business-unit VPCs, with each unit still managing its own subnets and firewalls
choices.rationale: Peering forbids overlapping subnet ranges, is not transitive, and does not exchange firewall rules, so control stays decentralized.

choices.text: One flat VPC inside a single project, where every application team holds the Owner role on the network
choices.rationale: Owner access for every team abandons least privilege and centralized control, and a single project removes per-team project boundaries.

choices.text: Separate VPCs for each business unit joined by a full mesh of HA VPN tunnels managed by the network team
choices.rationale: A VPN mesh is complex and bandwidth-limited, still leaves one firewall policy per VPC, and cannot join networks with overlapping ranges.

explanation: Grant the Compute Network User role per subnet so each team can use only its own subnets.

prompt: EHR Healthcare runs production databases on Compute Engine and Cloud SQL and must meet strict RPO/RTO and HIPAA-aligned retention. The team wants automated, policy-driven, application-consistent backups of Compute Engine disks across the organization with centralized retention and the ability to restore quickly. Which Google Cloud service is the best fit?

choices.text: A weekly manual copy of each VM disk image into a Standard Cloud Storage bucket, with retention tracked by hand in a sheet
choices.rationale: Weekly manual copies give a poor recovery point objective, are error-prone, and are not application-consistent.

choices.text: Kubernetes etcd backups of the container clusters, relied on as the only copy of the application databases and disks
choices.rationale: etcd holds Kubernetes object state, not the data in the databases and disks that must meet the RPO and RTO.

choices.text: Backup and DR Service plans and vaults covering Compute Engine disks and Cloud SQL, with enforced retention and application-consistent restore points
choices.rationale: Backup and DR protects Compute Engine, Persistent Disk and Cloud SQL through central backup plans, supports application-consistent recovery points, and vaults enforce WORM retention.

choices.text: A cron job that runs scheduled disk snapshot commands and keeps every snapshot indefinitely, with no retention rules defined
choices.rationale: Ad-hoc snapshots offer no governance or application consistency, and unbounded retention grows cost with no compliance control.

explanation: Match backup plan frequency and vault retention to each workload tier, and test restores against the RTO.

prompt: Cymbal Retail runs analytics on Google Cloud but keeps a large transactional dataset exported as files in Amazon S3. Analysts want to query that data with minimal data movement and without standing up and managing their own ETL clusters. Which approach best matches this multicloud analytics requirement?

choices.text: BigQuery Omni, which runs the BigQuery engine in the AWS region so analysts query the S3 data in place from BigQuery
choices.rationale: Omni runs the BigQuery query engine in other clouds (Amazon S3 and Azure Blob Storage), so data need not be moved into BigQuery storage.

choices.text: Export the entire dataset nightly to Cloud Storage and reload it into BigQuery before the analysts run their queries
choices.rationale: Nightly copies add movement, duplicate storage and staleness, which is exactly what the requirement tries to avoid.

choices.text: A self-managed Spark cluster on Compute Engine that reads the full S3 dataset again for every analyst query
choices.rationale: A self-run cluster brings back the operations burden and still pulls the data across clouds on each query.

choices.text: VPC Network Peering between Google Cloud and the other cloud, then querying the files over the peering link
choices.rationale: Peering connects Google Cloud VPC networks; it is neither a connection to another cloud nor a query engine.

explanation: Omni is limited to specific AWS and Azure regions and has query restrictions, so check the limitations before committing.

prompt: KnightMotives Automotive runs a 24/7 customer-facing telemetry ingestion service on Compute Engine with steady, predictable baseline load that rarely changes. The CFO wants the lowest sustainable cost for this always-on workload **without** risking interruptions. Which pricing/provisioning strategy is most appropriate?

choices.text: On-demand VMs with no commitment, so the team keeps full freedom to resize or stop the fleet at any moment
choices.rationale: Pure on-demand pricing gives up the discount that a predictable, rarely changing baseline would earn.

choices.text: Spot VMs that the service scales to zero between requests, relying on preemption to remove idle capacity
choices.rationale: Preemption is unpredictable and unannounced by default; a continuously running ingestion service cannot rely on it, and idle periods are not the issue here.

choices.text: Spot VMs for the entire fleet, because they carry the lowest hourly price of any Compute Engine pricing model available
choices.rationale: Spot VMs can be preempted at any time and are excluded from the Compute Engine SLA, which a 24/7 customer-facing service cannot tolerate.

choices.text: Committed use discounts with 1-year or 3-year terms, sized to the steady baseline of standard, non-preemptible VMs
choices.rationale: Commitments give steady always-on usage a discount (up to 55%, or 70% for memory-optimized, for resource-based CUDs) while keeping standard VMs that are never preempted.

explanation: Flexible (spend-based) CUDs range from 17% to 63% by service and term; cover the baseline with commitments and burst above it on demand.

prompt: A retailer runs latency-sensitive services on-premises that must call Google Cloud APIs (BigQuery, Cloud Storage) **without traversing the public internet**, and must also expose a **single global anycast IP** for a web tier running in multiple regions. Which combination meets both requirements?

choices.text: Private Service Connect endpoints for Google APIs over hybrid links, plus a global external Application Load Balancer
choices.rationale: PSC endpoints for Google APIs are reachable from on-premises hosts over Cloud VPN or Interconnect, and the global external Application Load Balancer provides one anycast IP for multi-region backends.

choices.text: Cloud NAT for the Google API calls, plus a regional external Application Load Balancer in each region of backends
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT translates outbound traffic from Google Cloud resources; it does not give on-premises hosts private API access, and regional load balancers have regional IPs.

choices.text: Public Google API endpoints protected by Cloud Armor, plus DNS round-robin across the regional load balancer IPs
choices.rationale: Public endpoints traverse the internet, and round-robin DNS neither gives a single anycast IP nor reacts to backend health.

choices.text: VPC Network Peering to Google's API network, plus an internal Application Load Balancer for the web tier
choices.rationale: Peering joins VPC networks, so there is no peering to Google's API network, and an internal load balancer is not internet-facing.

explanation: On-premises clients also need DNS that resolves the endpoint name to its internal IP; without a private zone, queries go to public DNS.

prompt: An organization uses a **Shared VPC** to centralize network administration across many service projects. Which statements are TRUE? Choose two.

choices.text: Resources in a service project, such as Compute Engine VMs, can be created in subnets that the host project owns
choices.rationale: Service project resources such as VMs and load balancers can use the shared network's subnets.

choices.text: Shared VPC removes the need for IAM grants, so any service project can use any subnet in the host project automatically
choices.rationale: Use of subnets is granted through the Compute Network User role, either on the whole host project or on specific subnets.

choices.text: The host project owns the subnets and firewall rules, which attached service projects then use for their own resources
choices.rationale: Administrators manage the network, routes and firewall rules in the host project, and service project teams deploy onto them.

choices.text: Each service project must create its own VPC network and peer it with the host project's network, which is how sharing works
choices.rationale: Peering is a different connectivity model; Shared VPC lets service projects use the host project's own network directly.

prompt: A team needs privileged node-level agents deployed as DaemonSets, Ubuntu as the node OS image, and hands-on control over node pool configuration. They want the least operational overhead that still satisfies these requirements. Which platform fits?

choices.text: GKE Standard, where the team configures node pools and can choose an Ubuntu node image
choices.rationale: Standard gives you node pools you manage and optional Ubuntu or Windows node images, and it does not apply Autopilot's privileged-workload restrictions.

choices.text: Cloud Run, with fully managed containers that scale per request and give no access to nodes
choices.rationale: Cloud Run is serverless: there are no nodes, DaemonSets, node images or node pools to configure.

choices.text: GKE Autopilot, with Google-managed nodes on Container-Optimized OS and allowlist-gated privileged workloads
choices.rationale: Autopilot manages node pools and pre-configures Container-Optimized OS with containerd, and privileged workloads need allowlisting, so node image and pool control are not available.

choices.text: Cloud Run functions, with event-driven source-based functions and no access to any cluster or node
choices.rationale: Functions are an even higher-level serverless abstraction with no nodes or DaemonSets.

explanation: The old explanation said Autopilot cannot run DaemonSets; Autopilot supports them. The deciding factors here are node OS choice, node pool control and privileged access.

prompt: A healthcare customer must guarantee that audit-log objects in Cloud Storage **cannot be deleted or overwritten for 7 years, even by project administrators**, to satisfy a regulatory retention mandate. What should you configure?

choices.text: Add an IAM deny rule on storage.objects.delete for every administrator account in the project
choices.rationale: Administrators can change IAM policies, so a deny rule is not an immutable control and does not stop overwrites.

choices.text: Place a temporary hold on each object by hand and release those holds only after 7 years have passed
choices.rationale: Temporary holds can be released at any time by anyone with permission and do not scale to every new object.

choices.text: Set a 7-year bucket retention policy, then lock it with Bucket Lock so it cannot be shortened or removed
choices.rationale: A retention policy blocks deletion and overwrite until each object is 7 years old, and locking makes the policy irreversible, even for administrators.

choices.text: Enable Object Versioning and add a lifecycle rule that deletes noncurrent versions after 7 years have passed
choices.rationale: In a versioned bucket a live version can still be made noncurrent, and versioning enforces no minimum age before removal.

prompt: A team built an HA VPN gateway to an on-premises router and wants Google's 99.99% availability SLA for the connection. They created two tunnels, both attached to interface 0 of the HA VPN gateway, each with its own BGP session on a Cloud Router. The on-premises router exposes two public IP addresses. Which change gets the design to the SLA topology?

choices.text: Add a third and fourth tunnel on interface 0 so that four tunnels share the same gateway interface and BGP session pair
choices.rationale: Tunnel count is not what the SLA keys on: every tunnel still leaves through one gateway interface, which remains a single point of failure.

choices.text: Replace the HA VPN gateway with a Classic VPN gateway that uses static routes over the two existing tunnels
choices.rationale: HA VPN requires dynamic BGP routing and is the topology that Google's SLA guidance describes; a static-route Classic VPN design is not that topology.

choices.text: Keep both tunnels on interface 0 but set the VPC network to global dynamic routing so that failover crosses regions
choices.rationale: Dynamic routing mode controls in which regions learned routes apply; it does nothing to spread tunnels across the gateway's two interfaces.

choices.text: Move the second tunnel to gateway interface 1, so each interface carries a tunnel, and keep BGP on both tunnels
choices.rationale: The 99.99% SLA requires at least one tunnel on each HA VPN gateway interface, paired with the matching peer interface, with dynamic (BGP) routing on every tunnel.

explanation: Pairing is interface to interface: tunnel 0 joins interface 0 to the peer's interface, tunnel 1 joins interface 1.

prompt: EHR Healthcare is retiring a colocation facility, but the data center that hosts its insurer-integration systems is not located in a Dedicated Interconnect colocation facility. The team needs about 2 Gbps of private connectivity to Google Cloud and wants the topology that carries Google's 99.99% availability SLA. Which design should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Partner Interconnect with two attachments in one metro on a single Cloud Router, using separate provider devices
choices.rationale: Two attachments in one metro on one Cloud Router fall short of the four-attachment, two-metro, two-Cloud-Router topology required for 99.99%.

choices.text: Dedicated Interconnect with two 10 Gbps connections in one metro, ordered through a nearby colocation facility
choices.rationale: The site is not in a Dedicated Interconnect facility, and two connections in one metro still fall short of the four-connection 99.99% topology.

choices.text: Partner Interconnect with four VLAN attachments spread across two metros, terminating on two Cloud Routers
choices.rationale: Partner Interconnect fits a site that cannot reach a Dedicated Interconnect facility or needs less than a full 10 Gbps; its 99.99% topology uses four attachments across two metros and two Cloud Routers.

choices.text: Partner Interconnect with one 2 Gbps VLAN attachment on a single Cloud Router, trusting the provider's redundancy
choices.rationale: A single attachment is one failure domain; the provider's internal redundancy is outside the SLA, which covers only the VPC-to-provider segment.

prompt: A company hosts Cloud DNS private zones for `gcp.example.internal` and keeps corporate DNS servers on-premises for `corp.example.com`. Over Cloud Interconnect, VMs in the VPC must resolve corporate names, and on-premises servers must resolve the Google Cloud names. Which configurations are needed? Choose two.

choices.text: Create a DNS peering zone in the VPC that names the on-premises DNS servers as the target of the peering
choices.rationale: Peering zones forward queries from one VPC network to another; they cannot target on-premises servers.

choices.text: Copy every on-premises record into a private zone by hand and update the zone whenever the corporate DNS changes
choices.rationale: Duplicated records drift out of date, and copies do nothing to let on-premises hosts resolve the Google Cloud names.

choices.text: Create a Cloud DNS forwarding zone for the corporate domain that sends the VPC's queries to the on-premises DNS servers
choices.rationale: A forwarding zone for the on-premises domain is the documented way for VMs to query corporate DNS while keeping internal Compute Engine names working.

choices.text: Create a DNS server policy with inbound forwarding so that on-premises hosts can query the VPC's private zones
choices.rationale: An inbound server policy gives on-premises resolvers a forwarding target to reach Cloud DNS private zones.

choices.text: Create a public Cloud DNS zone for the corporate domain and list the on-premises server addresses as its NS records
choices.rationale: A public zone is served from Google's public name servers; it does not make VPC queries go to private on-premises servers.

explanation: Allow source range 35.199.192.0/19 through on-premises firewalls and advertise a route for it, because Cloud DNS queries originate from it.

prompt: A team deploys a regional internal Application Load Balancer in us-east1 and needs the network resource that its Envoy-based proxies run in. Which prerequisite must exist in that VPC network and region?

choices.text: A reserved global anycast IP address and a Google-managed TLS certificate attached to the load balancer's target HTTPS proxy
choices.rationale: A regional internal load balancer uses a regional internal IP address; a global anycast address belongs to global external load balancers.

choices.text: A Cloud Router and a Cloud NAT gateway in us-east1, so that the load balancer's proxies can reach their backends
choices.rationale: Proxies reach backends over internal addresses, so NAT is irrelevant; Cloud NAT handles outbound internet traffic for private VMs.

choices.text: A VPC Network Peering connection to the producer network that hosts the proxies on the customer's behalf
choices.rationale: Load balancer proxies are allocated from a proxy-only subnet inside the customer's own VPC, not from a peered producer network.

choices.text: A proxy-only subnet in us-east1 (REGIONAL_MANAGED_PROXY purpose), with a firewall rule admitting its range to backends
choices.rationale: Regional internal Application Load Balancers require a proxy-only subnet, and backends must permit ingress from that subnet's CIDR range.

prompt: A game studio runs a custom TLS-wrapped TCP protocol, not HTTP, on servers in three regions. Players worldwide must connect to one anycast IP address, with TLS terminated at Google's edge. Which load balancer fits?

choices.text: Regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer in each region, with players choosing a regional IP address
choices.rationale: Passthrough load balancers do not terminate TLS, each has a regional IP address, and backends are limited to one region.

choices.text: Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer reached through a public DNS record that points at its private address
choices.rationale: An internal load balancer is reachable only inside the VPC network, so internet players cannot connect to it.

choices.text: Global external proxy Network Load Balancer, with an anycast IP, optional TLS offload and multi-region backends
choices.rationale: It is a Layer 4 proxy with a global anycast address, optional SSL offload and backends in multiple regions.

choices.text: Global external Application Load Balancer, using URL maps to send the custom protocol by path to each region's backends
choices.rationale: Application Load Balancers are Layer 7 and route requests by host and path; a custom TCP protocol has no URL to route on.

prompt: After acquisitions, a company has twelve VPC networks in different projects. A hub VPC is peered with each of the other eleven, yet workloads in two spoke VPCs cannot reach each other. The team wants any-to-any connectivity among all twelve without a mesh of peerings. What should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Add a Cloud NAT gateway in the hub VPC so that traffic from one spoke is translated and forwarded to the other spokes
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT translates outbound traffic to external destinations; it is not a router between VPC networks.

choices.text: Move all twelve networks into a Shared VPC host project so that peering becomes transitive for the attached projects
choices.rationale: Shared VPC lets service projects use one host network; it does not link separate VPC networks or make peering transitive.

choices.text: Install a router appliance VM in the hub and hand-maintain static routes for every pair of peered spoke networks
choices.rationale: Static routes cannot make peering transitive, and pairs of spokes would need hand-maintained routes that drift.

choices.text: Create a Network Connectivity Center hub and attach each VPC as a VPC spoke to obtain any-to-any connectivity
choices.rationale: NCC provides transitive, any-to-any connectivity across VPC spokes through one hub, with no pairwise peering needed.

choices.text: Enable custom route export and import on every hub peering so that routes learned from one spoke reach the others
choices.rationale: Peering does not provide transitive routing, and the custom route flags only change which static and dynamic routes are exchanged with a direct peer.

prompt: KnightMotives must upgrade connectivity between eight manufacturing plants and headquarters. Each plant connects to Google Cloud through its own HA VPN tunnels or Interconnect VLAN attachments, and plants must also exchange traffic with each other. The team wants Google's network as the backbone instead of provisioning links between every pair of plants. Which design fits?

choices.text: Build a full mesh of HA VPN tunnels directly between the eight plant sites, running BGP on each pair of site routers for failover
choices.rationale: A mesh needs a tunnel set for every pair of sites and its own BGP configuration, which is the provisioning burden the team wants to avoid.

choices.text: Build a Network Connectivity Center hub, attach each plant's VPN tunnels or VLAN attachments as hybrid spokes, and enable site-to-site transfer
choices.rationale: Hybrid spokes let dynamic routes from one site be re-advertised to the others, so plants reach each other over Google's backbone; each spoke needs its own ASN.

choices.text: Create a VPC Network Peering connection from the headquarters VPC to each plant's router so that routes are exchanged between sites
choices.rationale: VPC Network Peering connects VPC networks only; it cannot peer with on-premises routers.

choices.text: Terminate each plant on Classic VPN tunnels to a single VPC and rely on its routes to forward plant-to-plant traffic over the tunnels
choices.rationale: Classic VPN tunnels are not supported as NCC spokes, and nothing in this design enables plants to exchange routes with each other.

prompt: An HA VPN with a Cloud Router in us-central1 connects a VPC to the data center, and BGP is established. VMs in us-central1 reach on-premises hosts, but VMs in europe-west1 in the same VPC have no route to them. The VPC uses the default dynamic routing mode. What is the most appropriate fix?

choices.text: Enable Private Google Access on the europe-west1 subnets so that the VMs can reach private on-premises addresses
choices.rationale: Private Google Access gives VMs without external IPs access to Google APIs; it does not provide routes to on-premises networks.

choices.text: Switch the VPC network's dynamic routing mode to global, so that learned dynamic routes apply in every region
choices.rationale: The default regional mode applies dynamic routes in the Cloud Router's region only; global mode creates them in all regions of the VPC.

choices.text: Build another HA VPN gateway and Cloud Router in europe-west1 and add static routes there for the same prefixes
choices.rationale: Extra gateways and hand-maintained static routes add cost and drift; changing the routing mode needs no new connectivity.

choices.text: Raise the BGP MED on the us-central1 sessions so that europe-west1 instances prefer the learned routes over local ones
choices.rationale: MED influences which path is preferred among routes that already exist; it does not create routes in a region that has none.

choices.text: Tag the europe-west1 VMs and add a firewall rule that allows egress from those tags to the on-premises prefixes
choices.rationale: The VMs lack a route, not permission; firewall rules cannot supply a missing route.

prompt: A team is planning VPC Network Peering between a shared-services VPC and several application VPCs and wants to know what the design guarantees. Which statements are accurate? Choose three.

choices.text: Firewall rules are not exchanged between peered networks, so each VPC needs its own rules for traffic arriving from the peer
choices.rationale: Each network enforces only its own firewall rules; nothing is imported from the peer.

choices.text: Clients in one peered network can reach an internal load balancer that is hosted in the other peered network
choices.rationale: Internal load balancers are reachable across a peering, which makes shared services behind them consumable.

choices.text: Subnet ranges in peered networks may overlap as long as the VMs that use them carry different network tags
choices.rationale: Peering forbids a subnet range that matches, contains or fits within a range in the peer; tags do not change that.

choices.text: A firewall rule that targets a network tag also applies to VMs carrying the same tag in the peered network
choices.rationale: Tag-targeted rules resolve only to instances in the rule's own VPC network, even if peered VMs carry the same tag.

choices.text: Peering is not transitive, so two application VPCs that peer with the shared-services VPC cannot reach each other through it
choices.rationale: Peering does not provide transitive routing: networks peered to the same third network do not gain connectivity to one another.

prompt: Cymbal Retail's catalog-sync workers run on private GKE nodes and reach a supplier's SFTP endpoint through Cloud NAT. During the nightly sync, connections to the supplier fail intermittently even though the gateway shows plenty of free ports overall. Use the exhibit to choose the best fix.

exhibit.label: Cloud NAT gateway settings and nightly load
exhibit.content:
| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| NAT gateway IP addresses | 4 |
| Port allocation | Static, 64 minimum ports per VM |
| Worker VMs behind the gateway | 12 |
| Peak simultaneous SFTP connections per worker VM | about 300 |
| SFTP destination | 203.0.113.20, tcp/22 (one supplier endpoint) |
| Ports reserved across the gateway at peak | 768 of 258,048 |

choices.text: Raise the minimum ports per VM above the peak per-VM connection count, or use dynamic port allocation with a higher maximum
choices.rationale: Ports reserved per VM cap simultaneous connections to one destination IP, port and protocol; 64 ports allow about 64 connections where roughly 300 are needed.

choices.text: Add more NAT IP addresses to the gateway so that every worker VM receives extra ports toward the supplier endpoint
choices.rationale: More IPs enlarge the pool, but each VM still holds only its configured minimum ports, so the per-VM limit remains.

choices.text: Assign external IP addresses directly to the worker nodes so that they bypass Cloud NAT, accepting public exposure
choices.rationale: That removes the NAT limit but breaks the private-node design and widens the attack surface when a configuration change would solve it.

choices.text: Replace the single NAT gateway with one gateway per worker VM so that no two VMs share the same translation state
choices.rationale: Each VM already reserves its own ports; splitting gateways leaves the same 64-port allocation for each VM.

prompt: A trading firm stores transaction journals in Cloud Storage and must continue in a second region after a regional outage with no more than 15 minutes of newly written data missing. The bucket must fail over without manual intervention. Which configuration meets this?

choices.text: A regional bucket with a scheduled Storage Transfer Service job that copies new objects to a second region every hour
choices.rationale: An hourly copy leaves up to an hour of data missing and needs manual repointing of applications.

choices.text: A regional bucket in the primary region, since its data is already redundant across multiple zones
choices.rationale: Zones share one region, so zone redundancy does not protect against a regional outage.

choices.text: A dual-region bucket, for example NAM4, with turbo replication enabled for its two regions
choices.rationale: Turbo replication targets replicating 100% of new objects between the two regions within a 15-minute RPO, and dual-region buckets fail over automatically.

choices.text: A multi-region US bucket with turbo replication enabled, because multi-region buckets span more locations
choices.rationale: Turbo replication applies only to dual-region buckets, not to multi-region buckets.

choices.text: A dual-region bucket with default replication, relying on the typical one-hour replication of most new objects
choices.rationale: Default replication has a 12-hour RPO; most objects replicating within an hour is a typical case, not a bound.

prompt: A cleanup script deleted objects from a Cloud Storage bucket that still has its default data protection settings. Which statements are accurate? Choose two.

choices.text: Soft-deleted objects stop incurring storage charges the moment they are deleted, so keeping them costs nothing
choices.rationale: Soft-deleted objects continue to accrue storage charges until their retention period expires.

choices.text: Soft delete protects individual objects only, so a deleted bucket and its contents are gone immediately
choices.rationale: Soft delete also applies to bucket deletion, and a soft-deleted bucket can be restored during the window.

choices.text: Recovery is possible only if Object Versioning was on beforehand, because Cloud Storage has no other restore mechanism
choices.rationale: Soft delete is a separate recovery mechanism that needs no versioning and is enabled by default.

choices.text: Soft delete is on by default with a 7-day retention duration, so the deleted objects can still be restored
choices.rationale: Soft delete is enabled by default on compatible buckets with a 7-day retention period, and objects can be restored in that window.

choices.text: The soft delete retention duration can be set between 7 and 90 days, or soft delete can be disabled altogether
choices.rationale: The window is configurable from 7 to 90 days, and the feature can be turned off.

prompt: A lender must keep each loan document for 3 years after the loan closes, and the closing date is unknown when a document is uploaded. Which combination enforces this in Cloud Storage? Choose two.

choices.text: Turn on a default event-based hold for the bucket and release each document's hold when its loan closes
choices.rationale: A default event-based hold is placed on every new object, and releasing it resets the object's time in the bucket, so the 3 years count from closing.

choices.text: Place a temporary hold on each document at upload and release it at closing, which restarts the 3-year clock
choices.rationale: Releasing a temporary hold does not affect the retention clock, so the period still counts from upload.

choices.text: Add a lifecycle Delete rule with an age of 1,095 days, which counts from the day each document is created
choices.rationale: Age counts from object creation, not from the closing event, and a lifecycle rule is not an enforcement control.

choices.text: Enable Object Versioning so that earlier versions of each loan document survive until the 3-year mark passes
choices.rationale: Versioning keeps prior versions but enforces no minimum age and does not tie retention to an event.

choices.text: Set a bucket retention policy of 3 years so that no object can be deleted or replaced before reaching that age
choices.rationale: The retention policy sets the minimum time an object must stay, and releasing an event-based hold restarts that clock.

prompt: A media team wants to enable Autoclass on the bucket whose lifecycle configuration is shown, so that class transitions become automatic. They still want objects deleted after seven years. What should they do first?

exhibit.label: Current lifecycle configuration of the bucket

choices.text: Keep all three rules, because Autoclass runs after lifecycle rules and overrides any transition that conflicts with them
choices.rationale: The two features cannot be combined on one bucket in this way, so there is no precedence order to rely on.

choices.text: Keep the rules and set Archive as the terminal class, which makes the Nearline matchesStorageClass condition compatible
choices.rationale: The terminal class changes where Autoclass stops transitioning; it does not lift the restriction on SetStorageClass rules.

choices.text: Remove the two SetStorageClass rules, which cannot coexist with Autoclass, and keep the Delete rule for the seven-year expiry
choices.rationale: A bucket cannot have Autoclass together with a SetStorageClass action or a matchesStorageClass condition, but Delete rules remain allowed.

choices.text: Remove all three rules, since Autoclass blocks any lifecycle configuration, and run a scheduled job to delete old objects
choices.rationale: Only SetStorageClass and matchesStorageClass are restricted; Delete rules can stay, so a custom deletion job is unnecessary.

prompt: Altostrat Media must reduce storage costs for a growing library of video, audio and thumbnails while keeping content highly available. Which titles become popular again is unpredictable, and re-popular titles must not trigger retrieval or early-deletion surprises. Which configuration fits best?

choices.text: Add lifecycle rules that move every object to Coldline after 90 days and to Archive after one year
choices.rationale: Age-based rules ignore access, so a title that turns popular again incurs retrieval fees and the minimum-duration rules of the colder classes.

choices.text: Keep the whole library in Standard and rely on Cloud CDN caching to reduce the cost of storing rarely viewed titles
choices.rationale: CDN caching lowers serving cost for popular content but does not reduce the storage price of cold objects.

choices.text: Move everything to Nearline on upload, which has a 30-day minimum duration and a lower storage price than Standard
choices.rationale: Nearline still bills retrieval fees on every read and early-deletion charges, so hot titles can cost more than in Standard.

choices.text: Enable Autoclass on the bucket with Archive as the terminal class, so each object follows its own access pattern
choices.rationale: Autoclass moves objects to colder classes after inactivity and back to Standard when accessed, without retrieval or early-deletion fees outside enablement charges.

explanation: Objects smaller than 128 KiB, such as many thumbnails, are never transitioned and stay in Standard.

prompt: A pipeline writes intermediate files to a Cloud Storage bucket, reads them several times a day, and deletes them after 10 days. Which storage class is the most cost-appropriate?

choices.text: Archive, because its 365-day minimum storage duration is waived when a lifecycle rule performs the deletion
choices.rationale: Early deletion is charged whether the delete comes from a user or a lifecycle rule.

choices.text: Standard, which has no minimum storage duration and no retrieval fees for frequently read, short-lived data
choices.rationale: Standard has no minimum duration and no retrieval fees, which is what short-lived, frequently read data needs.

choices.text: Nearline, because its 30-day minimum storage duration lets files be deleted early at no extra charge
choices.rationale: Deleting before the 30-day minimum incurs an early deletion charge, and every read also costs a retrieval fee.

choices.text: Coldline, since its lower storage price outweighs the cost of its 90-day minimum for files removed after 10 days
choices.rationale: A file removed after 10 days is billed as if stored for 90, and daily reads add retrieval fees.

prompt: A fleet of GKE workloads spread over two zones needs a shared NFS file system for user uploads. The file system must stay available if one zone fails, and the team wants managed backups. Which Filestore choice fits?

choices.text: A legacy Basic SSD instance, which is zonal and offers fixed performance, with a weekly backup schedule
choices.rationale: Basic tiers are zonal, so a zone failure takes the file system down, and they lack the snapshot and replication features of newer tiers.

choices.text: A VM in one zone exporting a Persistent Disk over NFS, using the node's zone as the failure domain
choices.rationale: A self-managed NFS server on one VM is bound to a single zone and adds the operations the team wants to avoid.

choices.text: A Zonal Filestore instance in one zone, because backups can restore the data quickly after a zone outage
choices.rationale: A zonal instance is lost with its zone; restoring from a backup is recovery after downtime, not continued availability.

choices.text: A Regional Filestore instance, which provides resilience against zone outages, with backups enabled
choices.rationale: The Regional tier is built for regional availability and resilience against zone outages, and current tiers support backups.

prompt: A stateful database VM runs on a machine series that regional Persistent Disk does not support (it supports only E2, N1, N2 and N2D). The team needs near-zero RPO across two zones in one region and can fail over by attaching storage to a VM in the second zone. Which storage should the architect choose?

choices.text: A zonal Hyperdisk Balanced volume with a snapshot schedule every 15 minutes, stored in a second region
choices.rationale: Snapshots every 15 minutes mean up to 15 minutes of data loss, not near-zero RPO.

choices.text: Local SSD on the VM, with a replication agent that mirrors writes to a standby VM in the other zone
choices.rationale: Local SSD data is lost with the VM, and asynchronous agent replication adds its own RPO and operational burden.

choices.text: A zonal SSD Persistent Disk in the primary zone, attached in multi-writer mode to a standby VM in the other zone
choices.rationale: A zonal disk's data lives in one zone, so a zone failure removes it for the standby VM too.

choices.text: Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability, which replicates synchronously across two zones and supports more machine series
choices.rationale: It is the synchronously replicated, two-zone Hyperdisk option, supports additional machine series, and fails over by force-attaching in the replica zone.

choices.text: Regional Balanced Persistent Disk, attaching it to the VM even though that machine series is not on the documented supported list
choices.rationale: Regional Persistent Disk attaches only to E2, N1, N2 and N2D machine types, so this VM cannot use it.

prompt: A company keeps nightly Compute Engine disk snapshots in the same project as production. After a ransomware incident in which a compromised Owner account deleted resources, the CISO requires backups that attackers holding project Owner rights cannot delete before a minimum retention period ends. What should the architect do?

choices.text: Copy the snapshots to a Standard Cloud Storage bucket in the same project and let only the security team delete them
choices.rationale: Permissions inside the same project can be changed by a compromised Owner, so the copies are not protected against deletion.

choices.text: Run the snapshot schedule hourly and keep each snapshot for 90 days in the same production project as the disks
choices.rationale: More frequent snapshots improve RPO, but they live in the same blast radius and can still be deleted by the attacker.

choices.text: Remove the Owner role from every human user and keep a single break-glass service account for emergencies
choices.rationale: That narrows who can delete but offers no technical guarantee: a compromised privileged identity can still remove the snapshots.

choices.text: Protect the workloads with Backup and DR plans that write to a backup vault with an enforced minimum retention
choices.rationale: Backup vaults are isolated storage with WORM enforcement, so backups cannot be modified or deleted until the vault retention timer expires.

prompt: A bucket with Object Versioning accumulates noncurrent versions that raise storage cost. Which lifecycle capabilities can limit them? Choose two.

choices.text: A Delete rule that removes objects during their retention period, because lifecycle actions override retention policies
choices.rationale: Delete does not take effect on an object under an unmet retention policy or an object hold.

choices.text: Lifecycle rules that run the instant conditions are met, so unwanted versions disappear within seconds of qualifying
choices.rationale: Cloud Storage applies lifecycle actions asynchronously, so there can be a lag after the conditions are satisfied.

choices.text: A Delete rule using the numNewerVersions condition, which removes a version once enough newer versions exist
choices.rationale: numNewerVersions lets a Delete rule cap how many versions are retained for each object.

choices.text: A Delete rule using the daysSinceNoncurrentTime condition, which removes a version a set time after it became noncurrent
choices.rationale: daysSinceNoncurrentTime ages noncurrent versions out from the moment they stopped being live.

choices.text: A SetStorageClass rule that moves noncurrent versions from Archive back to Standard to lower their storage price
choices.rationale: Transitions run only toward colder classes, and Standard has the highest storage price anyway.

prompt: A team runs a managed instance group of API servers from an instance template. They need to move the group from e2-standard-4 to e2-standard-8 machines. What is the correct way to change the machine type for the group?

choices.text: Edit the machine type field on the existing instance template and let the group pick up the change
choices.rationale: Templates are immutable. There is no edit operation, so the group would never see a different machine type.

choices.text: Delete the group and build a new one, because a group's template can never be replaced after creation
choices.rationale: The premise is wrong. A MIG can be pointed at a new template with an update, so recreating the whole group is unnecessary and causes downtime.

choices.text: Create a new instance template with the larger machine type and apply it with a MIG update
choices.rationale: Instance templates cannot be modified after creation, so a new template applied through a rolling or selective MIG update is the supported path.

choices.text: Stop each running VM and change its machine type by hand so that the group adopts the new size
choices.rationale: Manual changes to individual VMs do not alter the group's target configuration, and the next recreation or autohealing event restores the template's machine type.

explanation: Treat templates as versioned artifacts: create a new one, then roll it out with maxSurge/maxUnavailable settings that match your availability needs.

prompt: A small team hosts a stateless web app in a runtime that App Engine standard supports. Traffic is near zero overnight and can jump tenfold within seconds during promotions. They want instances to start in seconds and to pay nothing for idle capacity. Which App Engine environment fits?

choices.text: The flexible environment, which always keeps at least one instance running
choices.rationale: Flexible cannot scale to zero. Its minimum of one instance is billed continuously, so idle hours are not free.

choices.text: The standard environment, but only after enabling SSH access and background processes
choices.rationale: Standard does not support SSH debugging or background processes. Those are flexible features, and they are not needed for this workload.

choices.text: The standard environment, which can scale to zero and starts instances in seconds
choices.rationale: Standard is built for sudden spikes and scales to zero, with startup measured in seconds, which matches the idle-overnight and burst profile.

choices.text: The flexible environment with a custom Dockerfile so that new instances start faster
choices.rationale: A custom runtime does not speed up flexible instances. They start in minutes, which is too slow for a tenfold spike in seconds.

prompt: A regional MIG of order-processing VMs shows clear weekday-morning and daily load cycles. New VMs take about five minutes to boot and warm caches, so reactive autoscaling leaves users with slow responses at 08:00 each day. The group has used a CPU-utilization autoscaling policy for six weeks. Which two actions address the problem? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Enable predictive autoscaling in OPTIMIZE_AVAILABILITY mode on the existing CPU-based policy
choices.rationale: Predictive autoscaling forecasts load from the MIG's history (it needs about three days of CPU-based history and uses up to three weeks) and scales out ahead of recurring daily and weekly peaks.

choices.text: Add a custom queue-depth metric and base predictive autoscaling on that signal instead of CPU
choices.rationale: Predictive autoscaling works only with CPU utilization. Cloud Monitoring and load balancing signals are not supported.

choices.text: Set the initialization period to roughly five minutes so VMs are added further ahead of forecast load
choices.rationale: The initialization period tells the predictive autoscaler how long an application needs to become ready, so it scales out earlier by that margin.

choices.text: Rely on predictive autoscaling to cover the one-off quarter-end surge the group saw once last year
choices.rationale: The forecaster recognizes daily and weekly patterns. It does not predict monthly, annual or one-time events.

choices.text: Shorten the initialization period to ten seconds so new VMs count toward utilization immediately
choices.rationale: A very short period makes the autoscaler treat unready VMs as healthy capacity and removes the lead time, which worsens slow starts.

prompt: A regional MIG of 12 checkout VMs (4 per zone) must keep at least 12 serving VMs at all times, and quota allows temporary extra VMs. The last template rollout, run with the update policy in the exhibit, caused a capacity dip and errors. Which change lets the next rollout complete without ever dropping below 12 serving VMs?

exhibit.label: Update policy used for the last rollout
exhibit.content:
# regional MIG, 3 zones, targetSize: 12
updatePolicy:
  type: PROACTIVE
  minimalAction: REPLACE
  maxSurge:
    fixed: 0
  maxUnavailable:
    fixed: 3

choices.text: Set maxSurge to 3 and maxUnavailable to 0 so each old VM is removed only after its replacement is running
choices.rationale: With maxUnavailable at 0 and maxSurge above 0, Compute Engine creates a replacement first and deletes the old VM afterward. A surge of 3 is one extra VM per zone, matching the regional default.

choices.text: Keep maxSurge at 0 and lower maxUnavailable to 1 so only a single VM is replaced at a time
choices.rationale: With no surge, each replacement still takes a serving VM offline first. Capacity drops to 11, below the stated floor, just more slowly.

choices.text: Set minimalAction to REFRESH so existing VMs are updated without being replaced or restarted
choices.rationale: A new instance template requires replacing the VMs. If the needed action is more disruptive than the minimal action, Compute Engine performs the required action anyway.

choices.text: Change the update type to OPPORTUNISTIC so the group replaces VMs gradually in the background
choices.rationale: Opportunistic updates apply only when you act on specific VMs or when the group creates new VMs through resizing or autoscaling. Compute Engine does not push them out.

choices.text: Set both maxSurge and maxUnavailable to 0 so that no VM is ever taken offline during the update
choices.rationale: If both resolve to 0 the updater automatically sets maxUnavailable to 1 so the update can proceed, so a VM still goes offline and capacity falls to 11.

prompt: A platform team creates a regional GKE Standard cluster whose node pool spans three zones and enables autoscaling with --min-nodes=2 and --max-nodes=5, intending the whole pool to stay between 2 and 5 nodes. At night the pool never drops below 6 nodes and a cost alert fires. What explains this, and what should they change?

choices.text: The location policy is ANY, so enabling node auto-provisioning removes the per-zone floor and allows 2 nodes in total
choices.rationale: Location policy controls how capacity is spread across zones. Node auto-provisioning creates pools but does not turn a per-zone minimum into a total.

choices.text: Regional clusters ignore the minimum until the pool is resized by hand once, after which the autoscaler can go lower
choices.rationale: No such behavior exists. The autoscaler honors the configured limits, and the floor of 6 is the direct result of a per-zone minimum of 2.

choices.text: The balanced autoscaling profile blocks scale-down, so switching to optimize-utilization will bring the pool down to 2
choices.rationale: The profile changes how aggressively underused nodes are removed, but it cannot push a pool below its configured per-zone minimum.

choices.text: The limits apply per zone, so the pool floats between 6 and 15 nodes; use --total-min-nodes and --total-max-nodes
choices.rationale: --min-nodes and --max-nodes are per-zone limits. Across three zones they allow 6 to 15 nodes. The total flags (GKE 1.24 and later) bound the whole pool.

explanation: Remember that regional and multi-zonal node counts are multiplied by the number of zones unless you use the total-node flags.

prompt: A Standard GKE node pool runs ledger-reconciliation Pods that need up to two hours to drain gracefully. The team wants to validate workloads on upgraded nodes and keep a rollback path before committing to the new version. Which two statements describe the right approach? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Use autoscaled blue-green, which is the generally available default for long-running batch workloads
choices.rationale: Autoscaled blue-green is a Preview option, and surge remains the default strategy.

choices.text: Choose blue-green on an Autopilot cluster, where GKE lets each workload select its own upgrade strategy
choices.rationale: Autopilot clusters use surge upgrades and the strategy cannot be changed. Choosing a strategy is a Standard node-pool setting.

choices.text: Stay on surge upgrades with maxUnavailable at 0, because GKE waits as long as Pods need before deleting nodes
choices.rationale: Surge upgrades drain for up to one hour and then forcibly evict remaining Pods, so two-hour terminations would be cut short.

choices.text: Make sure quota covers roughly double the pool's nodes for the duration of the upgrade
choices.rationale: Standard blue-green creates a full replacement set of nodes before draining the old ones, so it temporarily needs about twice the capacity.

choices.text: Configure blue-green upgrades so the original nodes stay available for rollback during the soak period
choices.rationale: Blue-green keeps the existing (blue) nodes available while workloads are validated on the new (green) nodes, which gives the rollback path and suits graceful terminations longer than 60 minutes.

prompt: A GKE Standard cluster runs fault-tolerant thumbnail workers. The team wants Pods on Spot VMs whenever capacity exists, on-demand VMs when Spot is unavailable, and a move back to Spot later with no manual work. The cluster autoscaler alone only prefers Spot when scaling up and cannot guarantee it. What should they configure?

choices.text: Separate Spot and on-demand node pools, with a CronJob that shifts replicas from one pool to the other every night
choices.rationale: This is manual choreography on a fixed schedule. It does not react to Spot availability and adds operational work.

choices.text: A Spot-only node pool with the cluster autoscaler location policy set to ANY across all zones
choices.rationale: The ANY policy searches zones for capacity. It does not provide a fallback to on-demand VMs, so Pods stay pending during Spot shortages.

choices.text: The optimize-utilization autoscaling profile, so the autoscaler favors the cheapest node type first
choices.rationale: The profile affects how aggressively underused nodes are removed. It does not rank Spot above on-demand or provide fallback rules.

choices.text: A custom ComputeClass that lists Spot first, then on-demand, with active migration, chosen by the workload
choices.rationale: Priority rules give ordered fallback, and active migration lets GKE replace nodes with higher-priority hardware (Spot) once it becomes available again.

prompt: EHR Healthcare is moving its containerized customer-facing apps to Google Cloud, but some Kubernetes clusters will stay in a colocation facility for years because of legacy insurer integrations. The platform team needs one consistent way to view, access and configure every cluster, including those outside Google Cloud, without giving cluster API servers public IP addresses. What should the architect propose?

choices.text: Convert every cluster to Autopilot so that Google manages the clusters sitting in the colocation facility
